Title: Hardware and software design of APEnetX: A custom FPGA-based NIC for scientific computing
Text:
Hardware and software design of APEnetX: a custom
FPGA-based NIC for scientific computing
Roberto Ammendola2, Andrea Biagioni1, Carlotta Chiarini1,∗, Paolo Cretaro1, Ottorino
Frezza1, Francesca Lo Cicero1, Alessandro Lonardo1, Michele Martinelli1, Elena Pastorelli1,
Pier Stanislao Paolucci1, Luca Pontisso1, Cristian Rossi1, Francesco Simula1, and Piero
Vicini1

Abstract.
In the High-Performance Computing (HPC) field, fast and reli-
able interconnects remain pivotal in delivering efficient data access and analyt-
ics. In recent years, several interconnect implementations have been proposed,
targeting optimization, reprogrammability and other critical aspects. Custom
Network Interface Cards (NIC) have emerged as viable alternatives to commer-
cially available products, which often come with high price tags and limited
or no customization options. In this field, the APEnet project has been and
continues to be engaged in developing custom Field Programmable Gate Ar-
ray (FPGA)-based NICs tailored for toroidal interconnection systems dedicated
to scientific computing and simulations: leveraging a custom network proto-
col and being easily portable and reconfigurable, it ensures adaptability across
various scientific domains spanning from High Energy Physics to Brain Simu-
lation; it implements a 3D direct torus interconnect, which nested in a multi-tier
topology, enables high path diversity, short cabling at low dimension and high
efficiency. In this work, we present the latest advancements for the APEnet NIC,
APEnetX, which integrates cutting-edge Xilinx Ultrascale+ technologies with
custom hardware and software components to enable Remote Direct Memory
Access (RDMA) functionalities targeting both the remote hosts and accelera-
tors such as Graphics Processing Units (GPU). A custom network protocol is
used, accompanied by Quality-of-Service (QoS) functionalities, to ensure effi-
cient data transfers between nodes even in the event of critical congestion states.
1 Introduction
The INFN APEnet project [1] is a long standing initiative focusing on the development of
custom network architectures and optimized Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based
Network Interface Cards (NIC) tailored for the communication generated by scientific appli-
cations running on distributed systems.
Over the past decades, several research initiatives have focused on FPGA-based NICs
addressing reprogrammability, easy portability and application optimization. Corundum [2]
is an open-source project featuring a high performance datapath, custom Direct Memory

project [3] aims to design power-efficient, programmable boards using ARM chips and FP-
GAs. FpgaNIC [4], designed for HPC and AI applications, crafts a Graphics Processing Unit
(GPU)-centric interconnect. The need for high-speed interconnect in High Energy Physics is
witnessed by the Felix [5] board which handles high data rate in several experiments. Other
initiatives focus on simplifying network design, such as EasyNet [6], which integrates a 100
Gbps TCP/IP stack using High Level Synthesis (HLS) tools, and NetFpga [7], which supports
rapid prototyping.
With respect to the aforementioned projects, APEnet stands out for implementing an ef-
fective light networking protocol, without the burden to be compliant with well-known net-
working standards like Ethernet or Infiniband. This choice makes APEnet highly versatile,
allowing the protocol to be easily adapted and used in different scientific contexts. Further-
more, APEnet implements a 3D (3-dimensional) Torus direct interconnect with up to 6 inde-
pendent links (named X-, X+, Y-, Y+, Z-, Z+) avoiding the use of external switch devices
to scale the computing node mesh. In addition, APEnet with its 3D Torus topology shows
several interesting features, e.g. high path diversity, short cabling, and low cost, that to-
gether with its reconfiguration capability make it a useful platform in network research field.
APEnetX [8] (Figure 1) is the latest version of the APEnet family, featuring a PCIe X16
interface and being prototyped on the Alveo U200 FPGA by Xilinx. APEnetX implements
Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) protocol where the data, without the intervention
of the Host CPUs, are directly transferred from the user-space memory of the source node
to the user-space memory of the destination node bypassing the kernel and minimizing the
transfer latency. Finally, APEnetX is equipped with Quality-of-Service (QoS) functionalities
to fairly assign network resources to running processes during congestion states.
Currently, APEnetX is installed in a four-node testbed, with each server featuring Sapphire
Rapids family Intel CPUs running at 2.7GHz, with PCIe Gen3 interface and hosting an
APEnetX prototype. The four prototypes are interconnected point-to-point using QSFP28
cables.
2 APEnetX hardware design
At the higher level of abstraction, the hardware stack of APEnetX comprises of two layers:
APEni – an interface between the PCIe bus and the FPGA – and the Network Intellectual
Property (IP) – which includes the network router, data link and physical layer of the APEnet
protocol.
2.1 APEni: PCIe host interface
APEni is in charge of implementing RDMA transactions over the host system memory of
interconnected nodes, leveraging the Queue-based Direct Memory Access (QDMA) subsys-
tem [9] and custom hardware components designed to optimize the communication.
In the QDMA subsystem, a DMA data transfer is initiated by means of descriptors and
is completed as soon as a completion is received. These data chunks, temporarely buffered
in software queues, contain all the necessary information for either the NIC or the Host to
retrieve or write data to memory, such as the virtual address or the number of bytes. In addi-
tion to multiple DMA engines for performing data transfers in both Host-to-Card (H2C) and
Card-to-Host (C2H) directions, the QDMA also includes an Advanced eXtensible Interface
(AXI) Memory-Mapped (MM) Slave and Master Bridge. This feature enables bypassing the
DMA engines while still leveraging the QDMA to generate and receive Transaction Layer
Packets (TLP) over the PCIe bus.

In a TX transaction, the host initiates the process by preparing a descriptor and writing
it to the FPGA. Once APEnet intercepts the descriptor, it processes the information, triggers
a DMA read from host memory using the QDMA engines, prepares the data packets, and
sends them over the network. In contrast, during an RX transaction, the QDMA engines are
bypassed to optimize performance: as soon as a new packet arrives at the destination node, a
descriptor is created, and an external DMA engine [10] writes the data into host memory.
APEnet offers several features that optimize data transfer between host memory and the
NIC, one of which is a Fast Send for Small Packets, designed to reduce latency for small
packet transfers. The implementation steps of this mechanism are the following: (a) the
address space of the QDMA AXI MM Bridge is remapped on the BAR4 of the PCIe config-
uration space; (b) an user-space application, exploiting the AVX512 instructions [11], writes
atomically 64B chunks of data on the BAR4 of the PCIe; (c) on the NIC, the Packetizer com-
ponent intercepts the 64B chunks of data coming out of the QDMA Bridge and forges the
packets. This mechanism can also support multiple concurrent processes running on the host,
as the BAR4 address space can accommodate up to 512 distinct address segments without
interference.
2.2 The Network IP
The Network IP implements a lossless torus interconnect by means of an optimized router –
APErouter – and a proprietary data link layer – APElink.
The APErouter comprises a full crossbar switch, a router and an arbiter. The switch
connects directly the intertile ports – the interface between then links and the crossbar – and
the intratile ports – the interface between the host and the crossbar. The router implements
a multidimensional torus topology, with a specific number of dimensions ranging up to 6.
Currently, APEnetX is prototyped on the Alveo U200, which has only two independent links,

using the Alveo V80 Xilinx FPGA, with a higher number of links supported.
APElink is a proprietary data link protocol designed to be lightweight while still offering
flow control and reliability features. The data stream of the protocol foresees the exchange of
six types of words:
• Magic and Start are special words used to establish a logical connection between neigh-
bouring nodes and notifying the upcoming arrival of a packet
• The Credit word provides information about the available space in the receiving FIFO of
the destination node, so that the overflow can be avoided
• The packet itself composed of Header, Payload up to 4 kB and Footer
Finally, APElink can detect corrupted headers by identifying up to two bit flips using the
Hamming code.
3 APEnetX software design
When selecting the Xilinx QDMA IP, we also evaluated the provided software for the ref-
erence design, which serves as a starting point for development. We then incorporated our
custom features support while maintaining the core functions to minimize the risk of incom-
patibility with future IP versions.
The software stack consists of several key components. The Linux device driver serves as
the communication bridge with the hardware, managing queue creation, register read/write
operations and memory pinning/locking. The queues play a crucial role in data transmission:
on the sending side, they are used to manage outgoing packet queues, while on the receiving
side, they support the completion mechanism that notifies the system when new data arrives.
Xilinx’s stack utilizes READ and WRITE syscalls along with a Netlink-based messaging
system for user-space to kernel-space communication. However, we opted for IOCTL as the
primary interface for our custom software enhancements.
The user-space library (LIBQCM) acts as the intermediary between user applications and
the Linux device driver. It is implemented as a dynamically linked library and provides a
wrapper for interacting with the driver. LIBQCM structures the data used in IOCTL syscalls
and includes optimizations to bypass user-space to kernel-space context switching, improving
performance.
To ensure software stability and validate new hardware releases during development, we
designed a series of non-regression tests. These tests also serve to assess the system’s overall
performance and verify compatibility across different versions of the IP.
Message Passing Interface (MPI) is a de facto standard for distributed computing and
HPC workloads, providing a widely adopted framework for interprocess communication
across different nodes in a cluster. By supporting MPI, we ensure that users can leverage
APEnetX through a familiar, standardized interface, allowing seamless integration without
requiring them to adapt to proprietary communication methods. OpenMPI’s modular design
allows third-party components to be seamlessly integrated, adding support for specific third
party hardware and networking architectures through BTL (Byte Transfer Layer) modules.
The BTL is a critical component of OpenMPI’s modular architecture, responsible for low-
level point-to-point data transfers between processes. By integrating our custom BTL, we
enable efficient interaction with our hardware, leveraging the QDMA-based communication
stack to enhance MPI operations.

4 Quality-of-Service features
The latest version of the APEnet card incorporates IPs designed to manage complex network
scenarios where multiple flows, while competing for the same resources (buffer and links),
may require different network performance guarantees or Service Levels (SLs), such as low
latency or specific bandwidth thresholds. Thus, we designed a mechanism to deal with this
scenario which falls under the name of inter-node QoS: the strategy responds to the SL by
prioritizing individual packets to meet the specific traffic requirements of each flow (Figure
2). For the purposes of this discussion, we will focus on the bandwidth requirement as the
primary SL target.
Figure 2: APEnetx with the support for the Quality-of-Service functionality. The different
colours refer to different Service Levels.
The inter-node QoS is applied at the APErouter component: each intertile port is com-
posed of a number of buffers equal to the number of SLs, so that each SL is managed inde-
pendently. The crossbar applies the prioritization of packets coming from the network, based
on the SL, applying a scheduling algorithm.
To help with the QoS task, the APEnetX design hosts a RISC-V based Rocket core [12].
Currently, it applies the scheduling algorithm based on static decisions; in the future we plan
to use the core to dynamically change the QoS settings based on the network congestion
condition.
5 Evaluation
We assess the APEnetX performance by measuring the minimum latency (Figure 3a) and the
maximum bandwidth (Figure 3b) achieved between two interconnected nodes. We performed
both synthetic tests as well as OSU microbenchmarks so that the whole hardware and soft-
ware stack, including the MPI implementation, could be evaluated. The latency is measured
in two configurations:
• Local Loop Test: the source and destination node coincides and the packets, after looping
around the switch return back to the source host CPU, without traversing the links;
• Ping Pong Test: the test involves two interconnected nodes, the latency measure includes
the software, NIC and link latency.
To be noted that the Fast send for small packet optimization allowed us to go from 5 µs to
2 µs latency in the ping-pong configuration, for packet size < 1 kB.

of four nodes. The scheduling algorithm is programmed so that a Weighted Round Robin

6 Conclusion
APEnetX is an FPGA-based Network Interface Card (NIC) designed for torus interconnects,
achieving sub-2 microsecond latency for small packets (< 1kB). We investigated and imple-
mented the hardware support for a Quality-of-Service (QoS) strategy, validating the design
through a physical APEnetX testbed with four nodes. Further design activities are ongoing
focusing on 1) the integration of special hardware/software blocks to optimize collective op-
erations; 2) the exploration of adaptive routing functions to enhance the QoS; 3) the design
of low latency interface to custom and off-the-shelf AI computing accelerators.
